The fan is like a centrifugal pump: when it comes nearly to synchronism it exerts a large torque, which must be overcome to pull into slip. abstract: Integrating Electric Meters. — Before giving a description of some of the integrating meters at present in use, it will perhaps be advisable to explain what an integrating meter is, since there seems to exist some doubt as to the meaning of integrating meter. Integrating meters register the sum of the electric quantity measured over a period of time. Thus if the intensity or strength of a quantity varies with time, the registration of an integrating meter will be proportional to the sum of the several products formed by multiplying together the quantity at a given time by the time during which it remained constant. In practice the electrical energy and quantity of electricity that has been made use of has to be known, and accordingly there is the integrating watt-hour meter and the integrating ampere-hour meter.

articleTitle: Discussion on items of practical experience
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Discuss the various methods of starting induction motors. Mr. R. H. Gould (Member): When Mr. Webb told us at the February meeting about the good results he had experienced with the Gorges type of automatically starting motor, I was one of those who stood up to say something unkind about this motor. I must say that I had not given my remarks sufficient consideration, and a day or so after the meeting it occurred to me that the trouble I had experienced with this type of motor was hardly due to the motor itself, as to the faulty protective arrangements available at the time I had my experience with these motors, viz., two or three years before the Boer War and a similar period after the Boer War. This was, as you will know, before the time of the general use of switches provided with overload trips. Both the 500 volt as well as the 120 volt three-phase motors were controlled by three-pole front of the board air break switches and lead fuses were used as protective gear; the strength of these fuses when used on a Gorges self-starting motor had to be so chosen so that if the motor did not start up straight away the fuses had to disconnect the motor from the supply, and it was in choosing the correct fuse that the chief difficulty was to be found. The margin between the strain on the fuses when the motor started up against full load, and the rating of the fuses, so that these would blow (if for some reason or the other, for instance, overload, the motor did not start up after the switch had been put in) was really insufficient, and the result was that, due to the continual strain when starting up the motor, one only of the three fuses would go, leaving the motor on single phase. Very often the remaining two fuses would not blow, as the motor would be standing still on the starting position; the result would be that a part of the motor, at least, would burn out. Now, I submit that this burn-out could hardly be debited to the motor, and with the gear available to-day, and with 20 years' further experience, I feel that there should be no difficulty in keeping a motor of this description running with a minimum of attention. With regard to the size of these motors, they were built in standard sizes up to 30 H.P., and quite a number of this size motor went through my hands at the time, and although these were installed on comparatively small plants, no trouble was experienced with regard to the voltage. I mention this, as I see from the March Journal that Mr. E. V. Perrow stated for motors above 20 H.P. it may become a serious matter to maintain the voltage at the motors in the vicinity, as a matter of fact, I am under the impression that the starting current of a Gorges motor would compare favourably with the starting current of a squirrel-cage motor and compensator starter.

abstract: (a) “ What are the relative advantages of steam and electricity for shaft sinking and winding ?” Prof. W. Buchanan (Past President): The relative merit of steam and electricity for winding has frequently been discussed at our meetings, the sinking of shafts electrically has not yet received much attention. A main object of our Institute is to extend the use of electricity, whenever it can be shown to be profitable, surely therefore it is fitting that we should examine with great interest the problem of shaft sinking in these fields to see if electricity offers advantages over the methods at present in use. There can of course be no doubt as to the ability of the electric motor to hoist the rock with greater quickness and certainty than is done with the steam engine, while the capital cost as well as the running expense of the electric system is the more favourable.
